green-peas-canned-cooked-with-butter-or-.title: Green peas, canned, cooked with butter

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green peas cooked with butter (or margarine) are a ready‑to‑eat product made from fresh peas that are blanched, drained and packed in jars with added butter to enhance flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas belong to the legume family and are a good source of plant protein.
Canning preserves the peas' nutrients for months without refrigeration.
Butter addition improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as A and K.
Peas are used worldwide in soups, stews, salads and side dishes.
Canned peas typically have a shelf life of 2 to 5 years.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of canned peas provides about 8–9 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas supply folate, thiamine and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Good source of minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium, phosphorus and potassium in peas support heart and nerve function.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and magnesium contribute to bone mineralization and may help prevent osteoporosis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to peas.

items.title: Added butter
items.content: The butter increases calorie density, which should be considered in weight‑management diets.

items.title: Potential BPA exposure
items.content: Metal cans can have trace BPA; avoid storing the product at high temperatures for long periods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be eaten straight from the jar, added to salads, soups, stews, or served as a side dish with meat. Warm gently before serving to distribute the butter evenly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and refrigerate, using within 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Kumquat is a small oval citrus fruit native to China. It is eaten whole, together with its thin sweet skin, which contrasts with the tart flesh. The flavor is sweet-tart, with a bright citrus aroma. Kumquats are eaten fresh and added to salads, sauces, jams, candied fruit, and drinks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kumquats are eaten whole, with the skin.
The name comes from a Cantonese phrase that can be translated as golden orange.
The kumquat originated in China.
In China and Vietnam, fruiting kumquat trees decorate homes at the New Year as a symbol of luck and prosperity.
Kumquats grow on small trees and are well suited to growing in pots.

items.title: Contain vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: The edible skin provides more fiber than the flesh of other citrus fruits.

items.title: Contain flavonoids
items.content: Citrus flavonoids have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contain essential oils
items.content: The oils in the peel give it its aroma.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Fresh kumquats are low in calories.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Kumquats are acidic and may cause heartburn or irritate tooth enamel.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Citrus fruits can cause allergic reactions.

items.title: Peel and treatment
items.content: Because the peel is eaten, the fruit should be washed thoroughly, and where possible choose fruit grown without pesticides.

items.title: Sugar in candied fruit
items.content: Kumquat jams and candied fruit contain a lot of added sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wash kumquats thoroughly and eat them whole, removing the seeds if they bother you. To soften the tartness, roll the fruit in your hands and press it lightly. Slice them into salads, make sauces, jams, and candied fruit, and add them to drinks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store kumquats at room temperature for a few days or in the refrigerator for two to three weeks. Do not keep them in tightly closed bags, as mold develops. Discard fruit with mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Shiitake (Lentinula edodes) is an edible mushroom native to East Asia, where it has been cultivated for centuries. It has a brown, umbrella-shaped cap and a tough, fibrous stem. Shiitake has a rich, savory, umami flavor and a meaty texture, and it is eaten fresh or dried in soups, stir-fries, and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shiitake traditionally grows on decaying hardwood logs and is now also grown on sawdust blocks.
Drying shiitake concentrates its flavor, which is why dried shiitake are prized for broths.
Shiitake are one of the most widely cultivated edible mushrooms in the world.
Their savory taste comes partly from natural compounds that give umami flavor.
The stems are usually too tough to eat but can be used to flavor stock.

items.title: Provides B vitamins
items.content: Shiitake contain pantothenic acid, riboflavin, and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Shiitake provide copper, selenium, and zinc.

items.title: Source of vitamin D when UV-exposed
items.content: Shiitake exposed to sunlight or ultraviolet light can be a plant-based source of vitamin D.

items.title: Contains beneficial compounds
items.content: Shiitake contain beta-glucans, such as lentinan, and antioxidants such as ergothioneine, which are being studied.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Shiitake are low in calories and add flavor to meals without adding much fat.

items.title: Shiitake dermatitis
items.content: Eating raw or undercooked shiitake may cause an itchy skin rash in some people, so cook them thoroughly.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Mushrooms may cause bloating or discomfort in sensitive individuals, especially in large amounts.

items.title: Buy from reliable sources
items.content: Buy shiitake from reputable suppliers and do not eat wild mushrooms unless an expert has identified them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Shiitake can be sliced and sautéed, stir-fried, grilled, roasted, or added to soups, ramen, risotto, and omelets. Remove the tough stems before cooking. Dried shiitake should be soaked in warm water first, and the soaking liquid can be used as a flavorful broth.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh shiitake in the refrigerator in a paper bag or a container lined with paper towels, where they usually keep for about a week. Avoid washing them until just before use. Dried shiitake keep for months in an airtight container in a cool, dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetable dip, yogurt based is a smooth sauce made from natural yogurt, fresh vegetables (cucumber, pepper, carrot, herbs) and seasonings. It has a light tang, refreshing flavor and creamy texture, making it perfect for snacks and light meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yogurt base adds probiotics that support gut microbiota.
Vegetable content usually exceeds 30 % of the total weight, boosting its vitamin profile.
Commonly used in Mediterranean cuisine as a healthier alternative to sour cream sauces.
Low fat content compared to traditional dairy dips makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.
Flavor can be easily varied by adding different herbs and spices.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Yogurt provides live bacterial cultures that promote digestive health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetables contribute vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and Vitamin D
items.content: Yogurt is a good source of calcium, supporting bone health.

items.title: Low in Saturated Fat
items.content: Compared with traditional sour‑cream based dips, this dip contains less saturated fat.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Fresh vegetables are rich in carotenoids and vitamin C, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free yogurt or plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: Milk Allergy
items.content: Those allergic to dairy proteins may react to this dip.

items.title: Sodium Content
items.content: Some versions contain added salt; consumers watching sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Limited Shelf Life After Opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the dip refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dip with fresh vegetable sticks, crackers, flatbreads, or use it as a sauce for burgers, rolls, and casseroles. It can be mixed into salads for a creamy dressing or blended into mashed potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Do not freeze, as the texture may change. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetarian stew is a hearty dish made from a variety of vegetables, legumes, and spices. It is rich in fiber, vitamins, and minerals, making it suitable for vegetarians and anyone looking to reduce meat consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional stews are cooked slowly to allow vegetables to fully develop their flavors.
Legumes such as lentils or beans add protein and make the dish more filling.
A mix of carrots, celery, tomatoes, and zucchini provides a wide range of vitamins and antioxidants.
Vegetarian stew can be repurposed as a base for cold soups or casseroles.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Legumes supply a complete set of amino acids essential for muscle and tissue health.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Vegetables and legumes provide B6, folate, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes, carrots, and spices like turmeric are rich in antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The absence of meat makes the stew suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, peas, or lentils.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Certain vegetables (e.g., spinach) can increase oxalate levels, which may be a concern for kidney‑stone‑prone people.

items.title: Potential sodium levels
items.content: Using prepared broths or soy sauce can raise the salt content of the stew.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stew hot as a main dish or alongside whole‑grain cereals, quinoa, rice, or bread. It stores well in the fridge for reheating and can also be used as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the stew in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly before consuming.
